doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: His own records and career today
title: First album Honeysuckle Breeze for Bob Thiele at Impulse
summary: His Impulse deal came first, then session with Wrecking Crew musicians.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: When you got ready to do a solo recording what came first, the band? The material? Or the agreement from a record company?

Well my very first album was for Bob Thiele of Impulse. And he, I figured out that he thought he could make me into kind of a pop saxophone player. I think maybe he thought he could get a pop instrumental hit from my album, my first album. It was called “Honeysuckle Breeze” which was an original tune composed by Ian Freebairn-Smith, one of the arrangers. I basically just walked in and played the charts that were put in front of me. So I guess I had signed the contract with Impulse, a typical record deal at that time. I think it was probably a deal for three or four albums, one per year, and of course the record company had the option every year to pick-up or drop me, and a royalty rate which was pathetically small by today’s standards. But on the other hand you know that was a different era. The record companies put a lot of money into marketing, promotion and advertising. And of course they did all of that at a certain amount of expense to them and they had big buildings with employees. I mean they had a big nut to pay. So I’m sympathetic on the one hand, but I didn’t expect to make money off my record. I hoped I would but again I think that probably the record contract came first, and then the session, the recording itself. As I say there was a stand with arrangements on it and I just played them with all these wonderful, again sort of 60s Wrecking Crew musicians. Carol Kaye on bass, Mike Melvoin on keyboards, Emil Richards on percussion, Jim Gordon on drums, and Glen Campbell on rhythm guitar. He was not yet a star and was doing rhythm guitar sessions as a session player, and I think Dennis Budimir was the other — I mean these were all the guys that were busy studio players in the pop music scene at the time. So it wasn’t a jazz record, although I played some licks that I suppose you could classify as jazz, but, so that’s how it happened.
